subjects.name: Chaco: building, gathering and continuing histories
subjects.place: Chaco Canyon, San Juan Basin, New Mexico, United States
subjects.geographicPrecision: Pueblo Bonito site locator. The regional Chacoan system extended beyond this point; no fixed political border is drawn.

interval.note: Regional frame. Pueblo Bonito construction c850–1150 and changes in the 1100s/1200s are distinct; this endpoint does not end Pueblo peoples or their ties to Chaco.

subjects.question: What connects a stone building, a traded ingredient and a living cultural landscape?
subjects.summary: Ancestral Pueblo people built great houses with planned masonry, timber and ceremonial spaces in an environment with limited rainfall. Chaco linked communities across the San Juan Basin and beyond. Archaeological chemistry adds evidence of cacao movement, while Pueblo accounts and contemporary community statements insist that this landscape’s history does not end when a regional center changes.

sections.title: Constructing a place to gather
sections.text: Pueblo Bonito was built in stages over roughly three centuries. Quarrying, shaping and placing stone, obtaining timber and organizing rooms were different kinds of work. NPS distinguishes this building history from Chaco’s broader regional system and describes a gathering place where peoples and clans shared knowledge and ceremonies. The surviving walls show impressive construction; they cannot, on their own, tell us the identity of every worker or occupant.

citations.locator: Great houses, construction, gathering and descendants’ accounts

sections.title: A chemical result with a limited reach
sections.text: Crown and Hurst’s 2009 study selected fragments representing five vessels from Pueblo Bonito. Three probable cylinder-jar samples yielded theobromine, interpreted as cacao evidence. The sherds were dated stylistically to about 1000–1125 CE. This supports movement of a tropical ingredient into the Southwest. It does not identify each intermediary, establish a precise route, or prove that every household drank the same beverage. The published study’s vessel photograph has separate copyright and is not reproduced here.

citations.locator: Sample selection and HPLC-MS results, pp2110–2112

sections.title: Changing centers are not disappearing peoples
sections.text: New construction slowed and Chaco’s regional role changed in the 1100s and 1200s. Migration and reorganization are different from extinction. NPS describes continued connections with other centers and with modern Southwest communities. Our c850–1250 window defines a selected regional context; the narrower c850–1150 dates for Pueblo Bonito describe construction of a building, not the duration of all Pueblo history.

citations.locator: Construction in stages, 850–1150 CE
Changes in the 1100s/1200s, migration and continuing connections

sections.title: Whose evidence belongs in the account?
sections.text: A 2025 resolution of the All Pueblo Council of Governors describes Greater Chaco’s continuing spiritual, historical and cultural significance to Pueblos and Tribes including Hopi. It is a community-authored source about living relationships with the landscape, not an archaeological date for a wall. Reading it alongside material evidence helps prevent the mistaken story that ancient construction left no connected people. The resolution is cited in its dated context, without claiming its policy requests describe current law.

subjects.name: Cahokia: city life and the problem of disappearance
subjects.place: Mississippi River floodplain near present-day Collinsville, Illinois, United States
subjects.geographicPrecision: Cahokia core-site locator; Greater Cahokia and other Mississippian communities are not merged into one state.

interval.label: Selected urban context, c. 1050–1400 CE
interval.note: Urban investigation frame used in the 2020 study; UNESCO describes broader occupation from c800 and an urban peak c1050–1150. The boundary does not assert that Indigenous life ended here.

subjects.question: How do we tell the end of an urban center from the end of a people?
subjects.summary: Cahokia was a large settlement with earthen monuments, neighborhoods, public spaces and working areas connected to a much wider region. Its history includes concentrated authority and ordinary labor. Archaeologists continue to debate later regional population patterns. Calling the city’s decline a vanished civilization would erase both differences in the evidence and later Indigenous histories.

sections.title: A city larger than one mound
sections.text: Monks Mound dominates many images, but UNESCO also identifies residential, public and specialized activity areas. The city’s working life cannot be reduced to a monumental silhouette. The Illinois research program studies a wider urban landscape with multiple precincts. This dossier locates the core and asks how concentrated settlement was built; it does not draw an empire around every place with related Mississippian material.

citations.locator: Greater Cahokia, urban core and earthmoving around 1050 CE

sections.title: Work, food and unequal power
sections.text: Agriculture, earthmoving, building and making things sustained the settlement. UNESCO interprets Cahokia as a complex chiefdom with surrounding centers and villages. That interpretation supports investigating unequal authority, but a site plan does not identify the conditions of every worker. The regional label Mississippian covers many communities and times. A similar ceramic form or mound is not proof that every maker was governed from Cahokia.

citations.locator: Description and Brief synthesis: agricultural society, chiefdom and activity areas

sections.title: What happened after the city changed?
sections.text: White and colleagues used lake-sediment fecal stanols together with archaeological, historical and environmental evidence to argue for renewed Indigenous population around Horseshoe Lake after the urban decline. Skousen and Aiuvalasit challenged that reconstruction and the attribution of particular populations, citing alternative explanations and regional datasets. This disagreement concerns how indirect evidence supports population history. A lake proxy is not a direct count, and this atlas does not choose a precise post-1400 population curve as settled fact.

sections.title: A later photograph and a continuing question
sections.text: The 1907 print shows a surviving mound long after the urban era, not an occupied medieval city. Its missing houses and people cannot be treated as proof that the wider landscape was empty. Compare the photograph, excavated activity areas and the disputed environmental reconstruction. The critical account keeps the city, the broader region, later populations and modern interpretations separate.

citations.locator: Earthlodge results and discussion

subjects.question: How can a building bring people together while its history remains open to revision?
subjects.summary: Ocmulgee’s Earthlodge joins surviving clay, reconstructed walls and roof, archaeological interpretation and Muscogee connections to an ancestral place. Its arranged seating helps investigate a public gathering space. New dating work changes the familiar story, while community collaboration challenges the idea that a gap in an old chart proves that people abandoned a place forever.

sections.title: Separate the surviving building from the reconstruction
sections.text: NPS identifies the clay floor as surviving ancient material, while the walls and ceiling were reconstructed in the late 1930s. The exterior photograph therefore shows an interpretation protecting an archaeological interior. It cannot reveal the exact ancient roof or who sat in each seat. Read the structure’s arrangement as evidence for gathering; a reconstructed doorway is not an untouched medieval entrance.

citations.locator: Reconstruction paragraph: surviving floor and late-1930s walls/ceiling
Specific Earth Lodge floor carousel item, NPS credit and absent exposure date

sections.title: A precise-looking date may hide an older method
sections.text: The collaborative study explains that 1015 is a median from older radiocarbon work. Newly analyzed roof wood instead indicates cutting sometime after about 1160; cane samples may also reflect an earlier structure. A latest preserved tree ring is not automatically the day a building was completed. This account retains the disagreement without drawing a false span between two unlike dates.

citations.locator: Results: Earthlodge; Discussion: Earthlodge and Public Buildings

sections.title: Gathering was part of political life
sections.text: The seating around the room and the more prominent platform support interpretation as a public council space. Elsewhere, NPS describes Muscogee political organization through towns, surrounding villages and councils. These are useful questions about organization rather than a recovered roll call for this particular room. Ancestral connections do not establish that every later office or custom already existed in exactly the same form.

citations.locator: Earthlodge and Council Houses: seating and public-building interpretation
Early Interactions: towns, villages and councils

sections.title: An archaeological gap is not a vanished people
sections.text: The study questions a simple site-wide abandonment story and works with Muscogee collaborators. Community history at the Council House in Okmulgee traces a bridge from southeastern homelands through forced removal to renewed political life in Indian Territory. That later building is not the Ocmulgee Earthlodge. Together these accounts invite a better question: what changed in a particular place, and what evidence shows continuing relationships?
